title: Modal Verbs and Stance Particles: Duty, Guessing, and Shared Knowledge
goal: Choose and interpret må, kan, skal, vil, bør, vel, jo, nok, and da by meaning, not just by dictionary translation.

objectives.statement: Choose and interpret må, kan, skal, vil, bør, vel, jo, nok, and da by meaning, not just by dictionary translation.

spans.value: Ingrid, Jonas, and Sara are preparing to spend the weekend at a cabin. Ingrid and Jonas are already in town, but Sara is coming by train. Heavy snow may affect the journey.
Du skal vel møte Sara på stasjonen?

blocks.translation: You’re meeting Sara at the station, right?

spans.value: Ja, men toget kan bli forsinket på grunn av snøen.

blocks.translation: Yes, but the train may be delayed because of snow.

spans.value: Da må du følge med på appen.

blocks.translation: In that case, you’ll have to keep an eye on the app.

spans.value: Det gjør jeg jo allerede. Toget skal være framme klokka seks, men det kommer nok senere.

blocks.translation: I’m already doing that, though. The train is supposed to arrive at six, but it will probably arrive later.

spans.value: Vi bør kanskje kjøpe mat før butikkene stenger.

blocks.translation: Perhaps we should buy food before the shops close.

spans.value: Ja. Sara vil sikkert være sulten når hun kommer.

blocks.translation: Yes. Sara will probably be hungry when she arrives.

spans.value: Kan du handle mens jeg pakker bilen?

blocks.translation: Can you do the shopping while I pack the car?

spans.value: Det kan jeg da. Men du må huske nøkkelen.

blocks.translation: Of course I can. But you must remember the key.

spans.value: Den har jeg jo i sekken.

blocks.translation: I do have it in my backpack.

spans.value: Bra. Da bør vi rekke ferga.

blocks.translation: Good. Then we should make the ferry.

spans.value: The practical problem is simple: plans depend on uncertain weather, shared responsibilities, and what each person already knows. The speakers therefore need more than direct statements. They indicate obligation, possibility, expectation, probability, and shared knowledge.
The small words matter. Compare:

en.value: The train is coming later.
The train may come later.
The train is supposed to come later.
The train will probably come later.

spans.value: These sentences concern the same event, but they do not make the same claim.

Norwegian modal verbs (modalverb) such as må, kan, skal, vil, and bør help a speaker present an action or situation from a particular point of view. The speaker may treat it as necessary, possible, planned, expected, or advisable.

Stance particles, often called modal particles (modalpartikler), such as vel, jo, nok, and da do not usually describe the event itself. They show how the speaker positions the statement in relation to the listener: perhaps the information is assumed, already shared, probable, obvious, reassuring, or relevant because circumstances have changed.
There is no reliable one-word English translation for every use. English may express the same nuance through a modal verb, an adverb, intonation, a tag question, or no separate word at all.

sections.title: Må: necessity or a strong conclusion

spans.value: Må often presents something as necessary.

en.value: You must remember the key.

no.value: Vi må dra før klokka sju.

en.value: We have to leave before seven.

no.value: Alle må bruke redningsvest i båten.

en.value: Everyone has to wear a life jacket in the boat.

spans.value: The source of the necessity can vary. It may come from the speaker, from a rule, or from the situation.

no.value: Du må sende rapporten i dag.

en.value: You must send the report today.

no.value: Besøkende må registrere seg i resepsjonen.

en.value: Visitors have to register at reception.

no.value: Vi må ta en taxi hvis vi skal rekke toget.

en.value: We’ll have to take a taxi if we’re going to catch the train.

spans.value: Må can also express a strong conclusion based on evidence. Here it means something like must in The lights are off, so they must be asleep.

en.value: It must be the wrong address.
She must have forgotten the appointment.

no.value: Ingen svarer. De må være ute.

en.value: No one is answering. They must be out.

spans.value: The distinction depends on what follows and on the situation:

no.value: Du må være hjemme klokka ti.

en.value: You must be home at ten.

no.value: Du må være sliten etter reisen.

en.value: You must be tired after the journey.

spans.value: The first sentence imposes or reports a requirement. The second draws a conclusion about the listener’s condition.

A common mistake is to assume that må always means an order. In the cabin dialogue, Du må huske nøkkelen concerns practical necessity. In Du må være sliten, no one is ordering another person to feel tired.
Kan can present a person’s ability.

en.value: Sara can drive in winter conditions.

no.value: Jeg kan hjelpe deg etter møtet.

en.value: I can help you after the meeting.

spans.value: It can also ask for or grant permission.

en.value: May I put my bag here?
You may go in now.

spans.value: In many B2-level situations, the important use is possibility.

en.value: The train may be delayed.

no.value: Det kan være glatt på veien.

en.value: The road may be icy.

no.value: Hun kan ha tatt en tidligere buss.

en.value: She may have taken an earlier bus.

spans.value: The same form therefore ranges from what someone is capable of doing to what may be true.
Compare the subject and context:

en.value: Jonas can drive to the station.

no.value: Det kan ta en time å kjøre til stasjonen.

en.value: It may take an hour to drive to the station.

spans.value: The first concerns Jonas’s ability or availability. The second concerns an uncertain possibility.
Kan does not normally signal that the speaker considers something probable. It only keeps the possibility open.

en.value: The train may be delayed.
The train is probably delayed.

spans.value: In the first sentence, delay is one possibility. In the second, the speaker considers delay the likely explanation.

sections.title: Skal: arrangement, requirement, or information from another source

spans.value: Skal frequently presents something as planned or arranged.

no.value: Jonas skal møte Sara på stasjonen.

en.value: Jonas is going to meet Sara at the station.

no.value: Vi skal dra på hytta i helga.

en.value: We’re going to the cabin this weekend.

no.value: Vi har avtalt tidspunktet: Møtet skal begynne klokka ni.

en.value: We have agreed on the time: the meeting is to begin at nine.

spans.value: Here the explicit agreement supports an arrangement reading. Skal can also present a duty, instruction, or formal expectation.

no.value: Du skal levere nøkkelen i resepsjonen.

en.value: You are to return the key at reception.

no.value: Alle skal være klare før avreise.

en.value: Everyone is to be ready before departure.

spans.value: This can sound firmer or more authoritative than a neutral description of a plan. Context tells you whether the speaker is reporting an arrangement or setting a requirement.

These are contextual uses, not always exclusive meanings of an isolated sentence. In particular, a scheduled event can be understood either as an arrangement or as information taken from a schedule. Explicit discourse cues are needed when that distinction matters.
Skal can also mark information attributed to a schedule, report, claim, or other source. The speaker does not necessarily guarantee that the information is correct.

no.value: Toget skal være framme klokka seks.

en.value: The train is supposed to arrive at six.

no.value: Den nye restauranten skal være veldig god.

en.value: The new restaurant is said to be very good.

no.value: Ifølge værmeldingen skal det bli kaldere i natt.

en.value: According to the weather forecast, it is supposed to get colder tonight.

spans.value: In the dialogue, the surrounding reference to the train app supports reading Toget skal være framme klokka seks as timetable information. In isolation, the sentence would not necessarily distinguish a scheduled arrangement from reported timetable information. Jonas then adds his own judgment: det kommer nok senere.
Compare:

en.value: The train is scheduled to come at six.
The train will come at six.

spans.value: The sentence with skal presents a schedule or arrangement. The sentence with vil sounds more like a prediction or assertion about the future.
A common mistake is to treat skal as a general future marker. Norwegian often uses present tense for ordinary future events when the time is clear.

no.value: Toget kommer klokka seks i morgen.

en.value: The train arrives at six tomorrow.

spans.value: Skal adds a perspective such as intention, arrangement, instruction, or reported expectation. It is not required simply because the event is in the future.

sections.title: Vil: willingness, prediction, or a characteristic result

spans.value: Vil can describe what a person wants or is willing to do. At this level, context is especially important because vil is not always a neutral equivalent of English will.

en.value: I would be happy to help.

no.value: Hun vil ikke svare på spørsmålet.

en.value: She will not answer the question. / She refuses to answer the question.
Would you like to come along?

spans.value: Vil can also make a prediction.

no.value: Sara vil være sulten når hun kommer.

en.value: Sara will be hungry when she arrives.

no.value: Det vil bli vanskelig å kjøre hvis snøen fortsetter.

en.value: It will be difficult to drive if the snow continues.

spans.value: It can describe a typical or expected result rather than one person’s intention.

no.value: For mye salt vil ødelegge smaken.

en.value: Too much salt will ruin the taste.

no.value: Denne løsningen vil spare oss for mye tid.

en.value: This solution will save us a lot of time.

spans.value: Compare willingness and prediction:

en.value: Jonas wants to pick Sara up. / Jonas is willing to pick Sara up. / Jonas will pick Sara up.

no.value: Jonas vil være på stasjonen klokka seks.

en.value: Jonas will be at the station at six.

spans.value: Without more context, the first sentence can concern Jonas’s wishes or willingness, but it can also predict what he will do. The second is naturally read as a prediction about his location.
Compare vil with skal:

en.value: Jonas is going to pick Sara up.
Jonas would like to pick Sara up. / Jonas is willing to pick Sara up.

spans.value: Skal presents the pickup as arranged. Gjerne supplies context that makes the second sentence about Jonas’s desire or willingness. Without such context, Jonas vil hente Sara can also predict that Jonas will pick Sara up. English will can conceal these differences, so direct translation is risky.
Bør often gives advice or presents the sensible course of action.

no.value: Vi bør kjøpe mat før butikkene stenger.

en.value: We should buy food before the shops close.

no.value: Du bør sjekke veimeldingen før du drar.

en.value: You should check the road report before you leave.
He should speak to the doctor.

spans.value: Bør is weaker than må when discussing action.

en.value: You must bring your passport.

no.value: Du bør ta med en varm jakke.

en.value: You should bring a warm jacket.

spans.value: The passport is necessary. The jacket is advisable.
Bør can also express a reasonable expectation or calculation.

en.value: The train should be here soon.

no.value: Vi bør rekke ferga hvis vi drar nå.

en.value: We should make the ferry if we leave now.
The package should arrive tomorrow.

spans.value: Here no one is advising the train, ferry, or package. The speaker means that the expected result is likely if the available information is correct.
Compare:

no.value: Du bør være på stasjonen klokka seks.

en.value: You should be at the station at six.

no.value: Toget bør være på stasjonen klokka seks.

en.value: The train should be at the station at six.

spans.value: The first may be advice about the listener’s behavior. The second is an expectation based on a timetable or calculation.
A common mistake is to interpret every bør as advice. Ask whether the subject can sensibly receive advice. If the subject is a train, package, result, or process, bør probably expresses expectation.
The five modal verbs can now be aligned around one situation:

en.value: Jonas has to meet Sara.

spans.value: The meeting is necessary.

en.value: Jonas can meet Sara.

spans.value: Jonas is able or available to do it.

en.value: Jonas is going to meet Sara.

spans.value: The meeting is arranged.

en.value: Jonas would like to meet Sara. / Jonas is willing to meet Sara.

spans.value: Gjerne makes Jonas’s desire or willingness explicit. Without gjerne or other context, Jonas vil møte Sara can also mean that Jonas will meet Sara.

en.value: Jonas should meet Sara.

spans.value: Meeting her is advisable.
The forms do not merely indicate different degrees of certainty. They frame different relationships between Jonas and the action.
A second alignment shows judgments about an uncertain situation:

en.value: There must be traffic.

spans.value: The speaker considers this the necessary conclusion.

en.value: There may be traffic.

spans.value: Traffic is possible.

no.value: Det skal være kø på denne tiden.

en.value: There is reportedly supposed to be traffic at this time.

spans.value: The information comes from an expectation or another source.

no.value: Det vil være kø når konserten slutter.

en.value: There will be traffic when the concert ends.

spans.value: The speaker predicts the result.

no.value: Det bør være mindre kø etter klokka sju.

en.value: There should be less traffic after seven.

spans.value: This is a reasonable expectation.

sections.title: Vel: inviting confirmation or softening a supposition

spans.value: Vel often indicates that the speaker assumes something is true and expects the listener to confirm it.

no.value: Du skal vel møte Sara på stasjonen?

en.value: You’re meeting Sara at the station, right?
We have enough food, don’t we?
This is the right road, isn’t it?

spans.value: The speaker is not asking from a position of complete ignorance. There is already an assumption.
Compare:

no.value: Skal du møte Sara på stasjonen?

en.value: Are you going to meet Sara at the station?

no.value: Du skal vel møte Sara på stasjonen?

en.value: You’re going to meet Sara at the station, right?

spans.value: The first is a more neutral question. The second presents the meeting as expected and seeks confirmation.
Vel can also soften an estimate or conclusion.

no.value: Det tar vel omtrent en time.

en.value: It probably takes about an hour, I suppose.
He is probably at home now, I suppose.

spans.value: The speaker tentatively presents a belief and leaves room for correction. Depending on tone, vel can sound friendly, doubtful, impatient, or challenging. The basic stance remains an appeal to what seems reasonable or expected.
Do not equate vel automatically with well. English well and Norwegian vel overlap in some expressions, but the sentences above are better understood through confirmation and tentative assumption.

sections.title: Jo: marking information as shared, evident, or corrective

spans.value: Jo often signals that the speaker treats the information as already known, obvious from the situation, or relevant as a reminder.

en.value: I’m already doing that, though.

no.value: Den har jeg jo i sekken.

en.value: I do have it in my backpack.

no.value: Vi kan jo ta en taxi.

en.value: We could take a taxi, after all.

spans.value: Ingrid tells Jonas to monitor the train app. His reply, Det gjør jeg jo allerede, corrects the implication that he is not already doing so. Later, Ingrid uses jo to reassure or correct Jonas by presenting the key’s location as immediately relevant.
Compare:

en.value: I have the key in my backpack.

no.value: Jeg har jo nøkkelen i sekken.

en.value: I do have the key in my backpack, after all.

spans.value: The factual content is similar. Jo presents the fact as shared, evident, or readily available and connects it to the current discussion; it does not by itself prove that the listener knew the fact beforehand.
Jo can also introduce an obvious reason or an available solution.

no.value: Vi trenger ikke vente ute. Kafeen er jo åpen.

en.value: We don’t need to wait outside. The café is open, after all.
You could call her, after all.

spans.value: The second example offers a solution as something accessible or obvious, not as a bare statement of ability.
Jo does not always mean that the listener literally knew the fact beforehand. A speaker can use it to frame the fact as something the listener can now recognize.

no.value: Det er jo helt mørkt her.

en.value: It is completely dark in here, after all.

spans.value: Both people can observe the darkness, so the speaker treats it as common ground.

A common mistake is to omit jo from interpretation because it lacks a stable English equivalent. The event remains the same without jo, but the social meaning changes: the speaker is appealing to shared knowledge or evidence.
Nok often marks the speaker’s own estimate that something is likely.

en.value: The train will probably arrive later.

no.value: Sara er nok sulten når hun kommer.

en.value: Sara is probably hungry when she arrives.
They have probably left already.

spans.value: Nok can occur with present, future, and perfect meanings. Its central contribution is the speaker’s probability judgment.
Compare kan and nok:

no.value: Det kan bli glatt i kveld.

en.value: It may become icy this evening.

no.value: Det blir nok glatt i kveld.

en.value: It will probably become icy this evening.

spans.value: Kan opens a possibility. Nok presents that outcome as likely.
Compare skal and nok:

en.value: The ferry is scheduled to leave at eight.
The ferry probably leaves at eight.

spans.value: Skal points to a schedule or reported information. Nok marks the speaker’s own estimate.
Nok also has a different use meaning enough:

en.value: We have enough food.

no.value: Vi har nok kjøpt for mye mat.

en.value: We have probably bought too much food.

spans.value: Word order and context help distinguish them. In nok mat, nok directly indicates sufficient quantity. In har nok kjøpt, it comments on the likelihood of the whole statement.
This distinction is important, but the focus here remains stance: nok as the speaker’s probable conclusion.

sections.title: Da: linking the statement to the situation

spans.value: Da has several grammatical uses in Norwegian, but here the focus is its role as a stance particle or situation-linking word. It often means that a statement follows from what has just been said.

no.value: Toget er forsinket. Da må vi vente.

en.value: The train is delayed. In that case, we have to wait.

no.value: Nøkkelen ligger i sekken. Da kan vi dra.

en.value: The key is in the backpack. Then we can leave.

spans.value: This da connects a consequence to a condition or changed situation.
In responses, da can make reassurance, contradiction, or insistence sound more engaged.

en.value: Can you do the shopping?
Of course I can.

no.value: Du har vel ikke glemt billettene?

en.value: You haven’t forgotten the tickets, have you?

no.value: Nei da, de ligger i lomma.

en.value: No, of course not; they’re in my pocket.
It’ll be fine, then.

spans.value: Tone and position matter. Da may sound reassuring, corrective, mildly impatient, or conclusive. The common thread is that the speaker presents the statement as fitting the current circumstances.
Compare a neutral statement and an engaged response:

en.value: I can help you.
I can certainly help you. / Of course I can help you.

spans.value: The second sentence reacts to an assumption or concern in the conversation.
Do not assume that every da means then in time. In Det kan jeg da, da is not locating the action after another event. It signals the speaker’s stance toward what has just been implied.
Consider the same basic statement with different particles:

en.value: You are coming tomorrow.

spans.value: This is a direct statement.

en.value: You’re coming tomorrow, right?

spans.value: The speaker assumes this and seeks confirmation.

en.value: You’re coming tomorrow, after all.

spans.value: The speaker presents the visit as shared or evident for the current discussion, whether or not the listener knew it beforehand.

en.value: You’ll probably come tomorrow.

spans.value: The speaker considers the visit likely.

en.value: You are coming tomorrow, aren’t you? / You will come tomorrow, surely?

spans.value: The speaker reacts to the situation and may sound insistent or surprised, depending on tone.
The particles are not decorative synonyms. They organize different relationships between the statement, the speaker, and the listener:

items.value: vel presents an assumption for confirmation;
jo appeals to shared or evident information;
nok presents the speaker’s probability judgment;
da makes the statement a response to the circumstances, often with reassurance, correction, or insistence.

spans.value: These meanings become clearer in connected conversation:

en.value: You’ve booked a table, right?

no.value: Ja, det gjorde jeg jo i går.

en.value: Yes, I did do that yesterday.

no.value: Restauranten er nok full i kveld.

en.value: The restaurant is probably full tonight.
Good thing we booked, then.

spans.value: Each particle performs a different conversational job.

Modal verbs and particles often occur together because they answer different questions. The modal verb frames the action or event; the particle frames the speaker’s relationship to the claim and listener.

en.value: You’re going to meet Sara, right?

spans.value: Skal marks the arrangement. Vel asks for confirmation.

no.value: Vi kan jo ta en taxi.

en.value: We could take a taxi, after all.

spans.value: Kan presents an available possibility. Jo presents it as an obvious or accessible solution.

en.value: She must be at home, after all.

spans.value: Må presents a strong conclusion. Jo points to evidence or shared reasoning.

no.value: Det vil nok ta litt tid.

en.value: It will probably take a little while.

spans.value: Vil predicts the result. Nok marks the speaker’s estimate as probable.

en.value: We should probably leave soon, shouldn’t we?

spans.value: Bør presents leaving as sensible. Vel makes the recommendation tentative and invites agreement.

no.value: Du kan da ikke kjøre i dette været.

en.value: Surely you can’t drive in this weather.

spans.value: Kan concerns possibility or practical ability, while da expresses a strong reaction to the suggestion.
When two stance-bearing words occur together, do not force them into one English phrase. Interpret each contribution.
Consider:

en.value: He is reportedly coming later.

spans.value: Even without examining every additional particle in Norwegian, the useful method is the same: identify what the modal says about the event, then identify what the particle says about the source, certainty, or relationship with the listener.
For the approved forms, use this compact procedure:

items.value: Ask what the modal contributes: må—necessity or an evidence-based conclusion; kan—ability, permission, or possibility; skal—arrangement, requirement, or information attributed to a schedule or report; vil—desire, willingness, prediction, or a characteristic result; bør—advice or reasonable expectation.

Ask what the particle contributes: vel—tentative assumption or confirmation; jo—shared, evident, or corrective grounding; nok—probability; da—a consequence linked to circumstances or reassurance, correction, or insistence in a response.
Read the sentence as one natural conversational move.

spans.value: Treating all future reference as vil
English often uses will where Norwegian uses present tense, skal, or no modal at all.

en.value: I’m coming tomorrow.

no.value: Jeg skal møte legen i morgen.

en.value: I’m going to see the doctor tomorrow.

no.value: Det vil bli dyrere neste år.

en.value: It will become more expensive next year.

spans.value: Use vil when prediction, willingness, desire, or a characteristic result is relevant. Do not insert it automatically for every future event.
Treating skal and må as interchangeable obligation words

en.value: You have to go now.
You are to go now.

spans.value: Må presents the action as necessary. Skal can sound like an instruction, decision, or assigned course of action. In other contexts, skal may simply report a plan.
Reading kan as probability

en.value: She may be at home.

spans.value: This says that being home is possible.

en.value: She is probably at home.

spans.value: This says that being home is likely.
Ignoring particles in translation

en.value: You know that.
You know that, after all.

spans.value: The core fact is unchanged, but the second sentence reminds the listener of shared knowledge. A translation need not contain a separate English word for jo, but the interpretation should preserve its conversational force.
Assigning one fixed English word to da

en.value: In that case, we’ll leave.
Of course you can manage that.

spans.value: The first links a consequence. The second reassures or corrects. Context and tone determine the natural translation.
At half past six, Ingrid calls Jonas.
Har Sara kommet?
Nei, toget står fortsatt utenfor byen. Det må være noe galt med signalene.

blocks.translation: No, the train is still outside town. There must be something wrong with the signals.

spans.value: Det kan ta lang tid, da.

blocks.translation: It may take a long time, then.

spans.value: Ja, men ifølge appen skal toget kjøre videre snart.

blocks.translation: Yes, but according to the app, the train is supposed to continue soon.

spans.value: Du blir vel på stasjonen og venter?

blocks.translation: You’ll stay at the station and wait, right?

spans.value: Jeg kan jo ikke dra fra stasjonen nå.

blocks.translation: I can’t leave the station now, after all.

spans.value: Nei, selvfølgelig. Jeg bør kanskje sjekke når neste ferge går.

blocks.translation: No, of course. Perhaps I should check when the next ferry leaves.

spans.value: Det er nok best. Vi vil uansett ikke rekke den første ferga.

blocks.translation: That is probably best. In any case, we won’t make the first ferry.

spans.value: The same forms now do connected work:

items.value: må marks Jonas’s strong conclusion about the signals;
kan keeps the possible length of the delay open;
the phrase ifølge appen explicitly identifies the source, while skal presents the train’s continuation as expected according to that source;
vel asks for confirmation of an assumed plan;
jo treats Jonas’s inability to leave the station as evident from the situation;
bør presents Ingrid’s action as sensible;
nok marks her proposed action as probably best;
da links Ingrid’s reaction to the new information.

spans.value: No single English translation captures this system. The intended meaning emerges from the event, the source of the claim, the degree of commitment, and the relationship between the speakers.

Now move to a different everyday situation. Nora has invited two colleagues for dinner. One colleague has sent a message saying that a work meeting is running late. The shops are about to close, the food is not ready, and Nora is unsure when everyone will arrive.

Without looking back, explain the central difference in two of these contrasts: må–bør, kan–nok, skal–vil, vel–jo, or jo–da. Then complete the authored retrieval task below. Produce two short Norwegian responses, each using one modal verb and one stance particle. Make each context clear enough that another speaker can infer the intended modal meaning and particle stance. The task uses only two combinations at a time, so you do not need to produce all nine target forms in one response.

prompt.value: Choose the interpretation that distinguishes må by meaning, not by a fixed English gloss.

options.text: «Du må huske nøkkelen.» expresses a conclusion from evidence; «Det må være feil adresse.» expresses practical necessity.
options.why: The contexts support the opposite interpretation.

options.text: Both statements express practical necessity: someone must remember the key and someone must have the wrong address.
options.why: The second statement describes an inference, not an order or requirement.

options.text: «Du må huske nøkkelen.» expresses practical necessity; «Det må være feil adresse.» expresses a strong conclusion from evidence.
options.why: The first statement requires an action, while the second infers an explanation from evidence.

options.text: Both statements express conclusions from evidence.
options.why: The cabin statement presents a necessary action.

stem.value: Cabin preparation: «Du må huske nøkkelen.» The office is closed and no one answers: «Det må være feil adresse.» Which interpretation fits both statements?

prompt.value: Choose the interpretation that distinguishes ability, permission, and possibility in these exchanges.

options.text: A presents possibility; B asks for permission; C expresses ability.
options.why: A concerns Sara’s capability, while C concerns what may happen.

options.text: A expresses ability; B asks for permission; C presents possibility.
options.why: The person can drive, the speaker asks whether an action is allowed, and the train delay is only possible.

options.text: All three statements present possibility.
options.why: The question about the bag is a permission request, and Sara’s sentence concerns ability.

options.text: A asks for permission; B expresses ability; C presents possibility.
options.why: The first two meanings are reversed.

stem.value: A. «Sara kan kjøre på vinterføre.» B. «Kan jeg sette veska her?» C. «Toget kan bli forsinket.» Which mapping is correct?

prompt.value: Choose the interpretation that identifies what gives each statement with skal its authority.

options.text: The first reports an external source, the second presents an arrangement, and the third gives an instruction.
options.why: The explicit cues support a different order.

options.text: All three statements present arrangements for the future.
options.why: The second is an instruction and the third is attributed to the weather forecast.

options.text: The first presents a speaker-backed arrangement, the second an authoritative instruction, and the third information attributed to an external source.
options.why: The surrounding cues identify an agreed plan, an instruction, and a weather-report source.

options.text: All three statements are direct instructions from the speaker.

Respond to the colleague and suggest what should happen, using one approved modal verb and one approved stance particle. 2. Create a different everyday situation, outside the cabin trip and delayed dinner, and write one short sentence another speaker could say. Use a different approved modal verb and a different approved stance particle. Make both contexts clear without copying a sentence from the lesson.

payload.judge_prompt: Check both parts separately and report evidence for every criterion. In part 1, require a connected Norwegian reply to the colleague's projector problem that makes a socially appropriate suggestion. In both parts, require at least one approved modal verb (må, kan, skal, vil, or bør) and at least one approved stance particle (vel, jo, nok, or da). The modal must contribute an interpretable event meaning such as necessity, possibility, arrangement, prediction, or advice, while the particle must contribute an interpretable stance such as confirmation, shared grounding, probability, or a consequence-linked response. In part 2, require a new everyday situation outside the cabin trip and delayed dinner, and require a different modal and particle from part 1. Accept natural Norwegian wording variations and do not require all nine target forms.
